clue.text: The scope of the old-style cuisine

definitions.text: The scope of the old-style cuisine

parts.words: The scope of the old-style cuisine
parts.note: a range is a scope, and the old cast-iron cooking stove of a Victorian kitchen gives the cuisine its range

explanation.surface: A food writer sizing up how far traditional cookery reached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scope' leads to RANGE; the cuisine is the kitchen, and the old-style stove that cooked it is the coal-fired kitchen range of British homes.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a pun: the range of cooking in an old kitchen was done on its cast-iron stove of that name.

clue.text: The, family, of a soft-hearted revolutionary

parts.note: a soft-hearted person is kind
a red is a communist revolutionary

explanation.surface: A family descended from a gentle-natured rebel.
explanation.definitionFit: One's relatives, taken together, are one's kin or family.

clue.text: Willing to try at the concluding point

parts.note: to try is to test

indicators.note: the concluding point of the little word 'the' is its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone happy to make an attempt when the end comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Willing' looks like eager, but it means making a will: a person who dies testate leaves one.
explanation.definitionFit: Having made a valid will before death is the legal meaning, so 'willing' is a pun.

explanation.surface: Labourers in the fields start a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: A haymaker is a wild swinging punch, as well as one who cuts and turns hay.
explanation.definitionFit: Hay-cutting labourers are farmworkers; a big round-arm punch is a blow of that name.

parts.note: nosy means curious, and these facial features stand out plainly on a countenance or face

explanation.surface: Odd traits openly tolerated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Countenanced' looks like 'tolerated', but a countenance is a face; 'Curious' plays on being nosy.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the features in the middle of a face, linked with prying curiosity.

clue.text: State in' the manner of University men

parts.note: à la is French for in the manner of
a BA is a Bachelor of Arts, a university graduate
an MA is a Master of Arts, another university graduate

explanation.surface: A condition described in the style of graduates.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabama is a US state in the Deep South.

parts.note: the Italian is shocking because he studied electricity in frogs' legs, not because he behaved badly

explanation.surface: A scandal about an Italian researcher.
explanation.walkthrough: Luigi Galvani made dead frogs' legs twitch with electric current; 'shocking' is electrical.
explanation.definitionFit: The eighteenth-century Bologna physician whose work on animal electricity gave us 'galvanise'.

parts.note: to win is to gain
Southwark is a London borough on the south bank of the Thames

explanation.surface: A painter takes a prize in south London.
explanation.walkthrough: Southwark is one of the boroughs of London, so it stands for BOROUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gainsborough was an eighteenth-century English portrait and landscape painter.

clue.text: " I'm broody ' said the hen. Pardon!

parts.note: I'm, put in the hen's words, is 'am' with the speaker left out
a broody hen wants to sit on a nest, so in the hen's own coinage she feels 'nesty'

explanation.surface: A clucking hen announces she is ready to sit, then excuses herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'said the hen' licenses the made-up word NESTY for broody, and AM for 'I'm'. The hen's 'Pardon!' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An amnesty is a general pardon granted to offenders.

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses the way the Bard handles justice as superficial.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Shallow is the foolish country justice of the peace in Henry IV Part 2 and The Merry Wives of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking depth means superficial; Justice Shallow is the comic magistrate in two of Shakespeare's plays.

parts.note: one who collects fleece for cloth, and by idiom a daydreamer whose mind wanders

explanation.surface: A forgetful person collecting fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: To go woolgathering is to daydream, from wandering the fields picking tufts of fleece off hedges.
explanation.definitionFit: A daydreamer is said to be woolgathering, literally collecting stray tufts of fleece.

clue.text: Zola's work includes one revised version of " State of Bliss '

indicators.note: the novel's title takes the other letters inside it, as a container holds its contents

parts.note: Nana is a novel by Émile Zola
one is the Roman numeral I
RV is the standard abbreviation for the Revised Version of the Bible

explanation.surface: A Zola novel is said to contain a reworked account of perfect happiness.
explanation.definitionFit: In Buddhism nirvana is the final state of perfect peace, and loosely any blissful condition.

clue.text: Split on the Adriatic by an Italian

definitions.text: Split on the Adriatic by an Italian

parts.words: Split on the Adriatic by an Italian
parts.note: Split is the Croatian port on the Adriatic, and the clue asks what an Italian calls it

explanation.surface: Someone divided over the Adriatic coast by an Italian rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split' looks like a verb, but it is the city in Croatia; its Italian name is SPALATO.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian name for the Dalmatian city of Split, once Venetian-ruled, is this form.

parts.note: a mark here is an emblem, the sort of sewn-on award a Boy Scout earns for proficiency

explanation.surface: Praise for a reliable fellow, a good scout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A good scout' reads as slang for a decent person, but it is a Boy Scout earning a proficiency award.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scout earns a cloth emblem for each skill mastered, a token of merit worn on the uniform.

explanation.surface: A military ceremony that includes a gun salute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salute of arms' suggests rifles; it is a hug, a greeting made with the arms.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking in means including; a hug greets someone with both arms.

clue.text: Cry up the rook in Cornwall

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word goes upwards, read backwards

parts.note: to cry is to sob
the rook in chess is also called the castle

explanation.surface: Praise lavished on a crow somewhere in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cry up' looks like praise, but 'up' turns SOB to BOS. Boscastle is a harbour village on the north Cornish coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Boscastle is a village on the north coast of Cornwall, so the clue names a place in that county.

parts.note: in a church service the congregation joins together in the spoken replies to the priest

explanation.surface: Joint action by the armed services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United Service' suggests the armed forces; it is a church service in which the congregation speaks together.
explanation.definitionFit: The congregation's set replies in a church liturgy are its part in worship.

clue.text: A drink for an Irish jaunt

explanation.surface: A tipple for a trip in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: A sidecar is a brandy cocktail; the Irish jaunting car was also called a side-car, its passengers sitting sideways.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy-and-orange cocktail bears the name, as did the two-wheeled Irish jaunting car.

parts.note: a lap belt runs across the lap, so the strap literally lies over the lap

explanation.surface: Asking where seat belts provide two layers of protection.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as OVER LAP: a safety belt goes over the lap, and an overlap is double cover.
explanation.definitionFit: An overlap is where two things cover the same ground twice.

explanation.surface: A shared public spot in an American town.
explanation.walkthrough: In American slang a joint is a bar, club or other hangout.
explanation.definitionFit: Shared means common; American slang uses the word for a bar or hangout where people meet.

parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice the clown Launcelot bids farewell to Shylock's daughter as 'most beautiful pagan, most sweet Jew'

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's clown about a girl he admires.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock's daughter in The Merchant of Venice is addressed in these words by her father's servant.

clue.text: Base to which I belong, by a fresh order

indicators.note: the letters are put into a fresh order, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone admits to a lowly place in a new religious order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like a noun, a headquarters; it is the adjective meaning low or dishonourable.
explanation.definitionFit: Base, in its sense of mean or dishonourable, is a synonym.

parts.note: read as taking off one's clothes rather than just changing into civilian dress

explanation.surface: A soldier coming off duty and changing into civvies.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip off one's clothes is to take off any uniform worn.

explanation.surface: A professor holding a chair in French military history.
explanation.walkthrough: A sedan chair is a covered seat carried on poles; Sedan is where France lost to Prussia in 1870.
explanation.definitionFit: A portable chair carried on poles shares the name with the French town of the 1870 defeat.

clue.text: Cab seen but not, in its present 'state

definitions.text: Cab seen but not, in its present 'state

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are not to be kept in their present arrangement

explanation.surface: A taxi glimpsed, but no longer in the condition it is in now.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal also defines: a word that means 'not present' is made from CAB SEEN rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Being away, not present, is what the word means.

parts.note: a jade is a worn-out horse, as is a hack
to be in front is to have led

explanation.surface: A worn-out horse took the lead, decked out in plumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jade' suggests the stone or the colour; it is an old nag. Hackles are the long neck feathers of a cockerel.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackles are a bird's neck plumes, so something supplied with them is dressed in feathers.

parts.note: a sewer is read as one who sews, not a drain, and the shield guards a fingertip from the needle

explanation.surface: A guard fitted over a drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' reads as a drain, but it is a person who sews.
explanation.definitionFit: A small metal cap worn on the fingertip protects a seamstress from the needle.

clue.text: Round Pond pear-tree may be heavier

indicators.note: the letters are turned round into a new order

explanation.surface: A pear tree beside London's Round Pond might outweigh something.
explanation.walkthrough: The Round Pond is the lake in Kensington Gardens, London, so 'Round' passes for part of a place name when it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To outweigh is to be the heavier, which is what the verb means.
